passage: In the small-town college at Tonk, the girls' bus had been cancelled for a month and nobody in charge seemed to care. Nazia, twenty, stood for student union president. At first it was about the bus. She loved the feeling when juniors called her "Nazia-di" and asked what she thought. After winning, she got the bus back in two weeks and everyone cheered. Then she noticed she was deciding everything: the fest theme, the posters, even who stood at the gate. At a meeting Bidisha, her closest friend, said quietly, "You didn't ask anyone about the theme." Nazia felt her face flush. She wanted to snap back. Instead she said, "You're right. Let's vote." It stung. She knew it was the right sting.

passage: Lindiwe had wanted to be head of the residence council at her university in Durban since first year. When she won, the respect felt like sunlight: people stopped her on the stairs to ask her opinion, and the warden began to call her by name. She fixed the broken laundry machines within a week. She opened the committee list again and added two open seats.

Subject: I won, and something's bothering me

Afreen Apa,
You'll have seen my photos. Your little brother is head of the cultural committee now. I stood because the fest was always run by the same three seniors and nobody else got a say. I wanted juniors and day scholars to have a voice.
And honestly, I love it. The principal calls me by name. People ask what I think before they decide things. It feels like standing a little taller.
But here's what's bothering me. Yesterday a first-year, Tanya, booked the auditorium for a poetry night without asking me first. My first thought was, cancel it. Who does she think she is? I actually had the email typed.
Then I remembered: that's exactly what I stood against.
I didn't send it. I went to her event instead, and it was good.
Apa, how do you want respect without wanting to control everyone? Tell me when you call on Sunday.
Zubin

I stood for the university senate because we women in our hostel had a curfew at eight and men had none. Nobody on the senate had ever lived with that rule. I thought, if I'm in the room, it changes.

Dear Lalit Bhaiya,
I've decided to stand for student council president. I wanted you to hear it from me.
Honestly, part of it is that I want to change things. The canteen prices, the library timings, the way first-years are treated. I'm tired of complaining in corridors. I want to be in the room where decisions are made.
And part of it, if I'm honest, is that I want people to respect me. To look at me the way they look at the current president.
But something happened last week that scared me. In our planning meeting, Priyanka disagreed with my idea for the poster, and I just overruled her. Didn't even listen. Later I thought: is that what I want power for?
Tell me what you think. You always know.
Francis

qa.a: The canteen prices, the library timings and the way first-years are treated.

qa.q: How did Francis feel after overruling Priyanka?
qa.a: Francis felt uneasy and a bit scared, worried about wanting control rather than service.

qa.q: What could Francis do to keep the wish for influence healthy?
qa.a: Francis could listen properly to disagreement, share decisions with the team, and keep the focus on what the group needs.

qa.q: How might Priyanka have felt when overruled?
qa.a: She probably felt dismissed and unheard, with her idea brushed aside.

Ritu, you asked for the college radio what it's like being hostel secretary. I'm Zainab, and I'll be honest.
I stood because I wanted a say. The mess food was awful, the Wi-Fi died every night, and nobody listened to us. I wanted to be the person who could fix things. And yes, I liked the idea of people respecting me.

One day Meenal, on my committee, said, "You're acting like the warden." That stung. She was right.
Now I have a rule: no decision without the committee. It's slower. But it's ours, not mine.

Week one. Rehana, twenty, gave her speech for student union president in the packed auditorium. "I want us to have a real voice." The crowd cheered. She felt a rush, like standing on a stage built for her.
Two weeks later. She won. Her first act was to extend library hours. Students thanked her in the canteen. She liked how people looked at her now.
A month later. At the committee meeting, Yamini proposed a vote on the fest budget. Rehana said, "I've already decided." The room went silent. Yamini said quietly, "Then why are we here?"
That night, Rehana couldn't sleep. She had wanted to lead. Somewhere she'd started wanting to control.
The next morning she called the meeting again and said, "Let's vote."

With only two days until the college union elections, Alka's campaign posters were torn in the rain and she had no money for new ones. She stood in the canteen giving her speech without a mic, voice cracking over the noise.
"I want to fix the broken hostel water pumps and get a fair fee-refund system," she said. "And yes, I want a seat at the table where decisions happen."
Her friend Rajni watched, arms folded. Later she said, "You know what worries me? Last week you told the second-years they'd 'better vote for you if they want the new wing'. That sounded like a threat."
Alka's cheeks went hot. "I didn't mean it like that."
"Then don't say it like that."
Alka looked at her torn posters. She wanted to lead. She didn't want to become someone people feared.

Arnab had been elected sports secretary at his Kolkata college in July. By October, the football ground finally had working floodlights, and the girls' team had its own practice slot. People stopped him in corridors to say thank you. He liked that more than he admitted.
Then Sangeeta, the girls' captain, asked for a change in the match schedule.
"No," Arnab said, before she finished.
"You didn't even hear why."
"I decide the schedule. That's the job."
She looked at him for a long moment. "Last month you said you wanted everyone to have a voice."
Arnab felt a flash of irritation, then something colder: she was right. He took a breath. "Okay. Tell me why."

The first month went well; I got a timetable clash fixed and people started saying, 'Ask Rukmini.' I liked that more than I expected. Mentor's note, first-year orientation week.
Mahima volunteered to lead her group of twelve for the campus clean-up and did it well: she split the tasks fairly, checked on the slowest team and thanked each person by name. At the wrap-up she told me she plans to stand for the students' council next year. 'I want to be the one they come to,' she said. Later, though, I watched her take the clipboard from Akash, who had been assigned sign-in, and redo his list without asking him. Akash went silent for the rest of the afternoon. I spoke to Mahima privately afterwards, praising her organising and asking how Akash might have felt. She paused, then went to return the clipboard. I'll check in with both of them next week.

qa.q: How many people were in Mahima's group for the clean-up?
qa.a: Her group of twelve.

qa.q: What does Mahima's wish to be 'the one they come to' suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Mahima feels ambitious and proud of leading, wanting respect and influence among her peers.

qa.q: Was the mentor's private talk with Mahima a good step? Why?
qa.a: Yes; it praised her real skills while helping her notice how taking over felt to Akash, so she could correct it herself without being shamed.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when his list was taken and redone?
qa.a: Akash probably felt belittled and embarrassed, which is why he went silent for the rest of the afternoon.

23 December, hostel, 11 pm
Filed my nomination for student council president today, right before everyone leaves for the Christmas break. My hands were shaking when I signed.
Why am I doing this? Honestly, two reasons. One: the girls' hostel curfew is ridiculous and nobody fights it properly. I can. Two: I loved it when the whole canteen went quiet during my debate speech. I want that. I want people to listen when I talk.
Tonight I made a list of who would be on my team. Then I noticed I had crossed out Akash, not because he's bad, but because he argues with me. That felt ugly. A council of people who agree with me isn't leadership, it's a fan club. Adding him back. Chandrika, remember why you started.

qa.q: What position did Chandrika file a nomination for?
qa.a: Student council president.

qa.q: Why did crossing out Akash feel ugly to Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika felt uneasy and ashamed on noticing the wish for influence sliding into control, cutting Akash only because he disagrees.

qa.q: What small check could help Chandrika stay on the serving side of power?
qa.a: Keep people who disagree on the team, as Chandrika did with Akash, and keep asking whether each decision serves the group or only the wish to be listened to.

qa.q: What would change for the council if Akash stayed off the list?
qa.a: It would lose someone who questions and argues, turning into a fan club that agrees with Chandrika instead of testing ideas.
